$$\alpha = \frac{L_2 - L_1}{L_1(T_2 - T_1)}$$

Here, $L_1 = 10\text{ m}$

$$L_2 = 10.0167\text{ m}$$
$$T_2 = 120^\circ\text{ C}$$
$$T_1 = 20^\circ\text{ C}$$

$$\alpha = \frac{10.0167\text{ m} - 10\text{ m}}{10\text{ m}(120^\circ\text{ C} - 20^\circ\text{ C})} = 16.7 \times 10^{-6}\text{ }^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$$

You have seen from the above examples that actually the value of the co-efficient of expansion of solids is very small. For this reason, the three different co-efficients $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ were not necessary. For working we could explain the co-efficient of linear expansion only. For example let us assume the matter of area expansion.

We see:
$$A_2 = A_1 + \beta A_1 (T_2 - T_1)$$

But area $A_1$ is the product of length and width and if we consider the area of a square whose length is $L_1$, then its area, after increasing the temperature, will be

$$A_2 = L_2^2 = [L_1 + \alpha L_1 (T_2 - T_1)]^2$$

Or

$$A_2 = L_1^2 + 2\alpha L_1^2 (T_2 - T_1) + \alpha^2 L_1^2 (T_2 - T_1)^2$$

But

$$A_1 = L_1^2$$

So,

$$A_2 = A_1 + 2\alpha A_1 (T_2 - T_1) + \alpha^2 A_1 (T_2 - T_1)^2$$

We have seen that the value of $\alpha$ is very small, so the value of $\alpha^2$ is smaller. In fact it is so small that if we avoid the whole part with $\alpha^2$, then no problem will arise in our analysis or calculation. So we can write:

$$A_2 = A_1 + 2\alpha A_1 (T_2 - T_1)$$

But we know,

$$A_2 = A_1 + \beta A_1 (T_2 - T_1)$$
